raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy for selected patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF) who remain limited despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and who are not candidates for, or have not responded to, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Contemporary HF guidelines emphasize four-pillar pharmacotherapy and conventional device therapy, but a substantial subgroup with persistent symptoms, reduced or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and narrow QRS duration has limited device-based options [1,2]. CCM addresses this gap by delivering relatively high-voltage, biphasic, non-excitatory electrical impulses to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period; because stimulation occurs after depolarization, it is intended to augment contractility without initiating a new action potential or producing ventricular resynchronization [3-7].

The biological rationale for CCM is supported by preclinical and translational studies. Early work showed that electrical currents applied during refractoriness could acutely increase myocardial contractile performance in vitro and in vivo [3-5]. In canine HF models, CCM improved left ventricular function and attenuated remodeling without the signal pattern of conventional pacing [6,8]. Human and animal studies suggest that CCM can increase intracellular calcium cycling efficiency and reverse aspects of HF-associated fetal gene expression, including pathways involving sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium handling and contractile proteins [7,26,27]. Unlike catecholaminergic inotropes, CCM has not consistently increased myocardial oxygen consumption in experimental settings, a distinction that underpins its long-term therapeutic appeal [26].

Clinical experience began with acute hemodynamic and early chronic feasibility studies. Pappone and colleagues demonstrated improved left ventricular pressure development and regional function when CCM currents were applied in patients with ischemic or idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy [9]. Subsequent pilot studies using implantable systems showed feasibility, acceptable procedural safety, and signals of improvement in symptoms, exercise capacity, and quality of life [10]. The randomized double-blind crossover study by Borggrefe et al. found significantly better peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores during active CCM than during sham periods [11]. The larger FIX-HF-5 randomized trial did not meet all primary efficacy end points in the overall cohort but generated an important hypothesis that patients with moderately reduced LVEF and narrow QRS might benefit most [12,13].

This hypothesis was tested in FIX-HF-5C, which enrolled symptomatic patients with LVEF 25–45% and narrow QRS who were not candidates for CRT. CCM improved peak oxygen consumption, 6-minute walk distance, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, and quality-of-life measures, with acceptable device-related safety [14]. A later study of a two-lead Optimizer system supported similar performance while reducing lead burden compared with earlier three-lead systems [15]. Registry analyses extended these observations: CCM-REG and related cohorts reported sustained improvements in NYHA class, quality of life, LVEF, and reductions in HF hospitalization compared with patients’ pre-implant course or risk-model expectations [16-19]. Smaller studies also explored programming duration, use in permanent atrial fibrillation, and adjunctive therapy after CRT non-response [20-22].

Meta-analyses broadly support modest but consistent functional benefit. Individual-patient and aggregate-data analyses have shown improvements in peak oxygen consumption and HF-related quality of life, although effects on mortality remain uncertain because trials were not powered for survival and many observational comparisons are susceptible to confounding [23-25]. The most appropriate candidates are generally ambulatory patients with persistent NYHA class III symptoms, optimized medical therapy, LVEF approximately 25–45%, and QRS duration below CRT thresholds, particularly when LVEF is in the 35–45% range [14,16,23]. Emerging data in HF with mildly reduced EF and real-world US cohorts suggest potential expansion, but definitive randomized outcome trials remain needed [29,30].

Practical limitations include procedural risks typical of transvenous devices, lead dislodgement, infection, generator maintenance and recharging, device–device interaction with defibrillators, and the need for specialized programming [15,28]. CCM should not be viewed as a substitute for GDMT, defibrillator therapy when indicated, CRT in patients meeting criteria, valve intervention, revascularization, or advanced HF referral. Rather, CCM is best conceptualized as an adjunctive bioelectronic therapy aimed at symptoms and functional capacity in a carefully selected narrow-QRS HF population. Future research should clarify effects on hospitalization and survival, refine predictors of response, define utility in atrial fibrillation and HF with mildly reduced or preserved EF, and evaluate integrated CCM-defibrillator platforms.
